headline: The Data Gap at the Heart of Global Liquidity Analysis
lede: A short reply in a macro data exchange names a genuine and underappreciated problem: there is no authoritative, freely accessible dataset for global M2 — the aggregate of broad money across the world's major central banks. What most charts label “M2 is rising” is the American figure alone, roughly $21 trillion of a $123 trillion global pool. The institutional workaround — Bloomberg's commercial composite index — costs tens of thousands of dollars annually, leaving independent analysts to hand-aggregate from central bank releases with no standard methodology.
body:
**M2** — in American usage — encompasses currency in circulation, checking deposits, small-denomination certificates of deposit, and retail money-market fund shares, as measured by the Federal Reserve's weekly H.6 release. The Fed itself has not used M2 as a policy target since the early 1990s. Yet it remains the default proxy for “money in the system” in charts linking monetary expansion to asset prices. The structural problem the tweet names is real: the Fed publishes clean weekly data because it is one central bank measuring one monetary zone. Constructing an equivalent global figure requires aggregating releases from the *ECB*, the People's Bank of China (*PBOC*), the Bank of Japan, and many more — each using different definitions, carrying different reporting lags, and denominated in currencies that must be converted at fluctuating exchange rates.

Practitioner aggregations of **global M2** typically anchor on four central banks — the Fed, ECB, PBOC, and Bank of Japan — because together they account for the majority of world GDP. MacroMicro, a financial data firm, publishes this four-bank aggregate freely but warns of a built-in distortion: a falling dollar mechanically inflates the dollar-denominated M2 of every other country even if no new money was created. Lyn Alden, a macro analyst who tracks an eight-country global M2 (adding the UK, Canada, Russia, and Australia), has found that this broader measure moves in the same direction as risk assets — equities, gold, Bitcoin — in roughly 83% of observed twelve-month periods, higher than any other major asset class. That correlation is stronger than the US-only figure, which is pulled by domestic mechanics such as *Treasury General Account* drawdowns and Federal Reserve *overnight reverse repurchase agreements* that say little about conditions elsewhere.

No single authoritative, freely accessible global M2 dataset exists. The Bank for International Settlements publishes *Global Liquidity Indicators* quarterly, but these track cross-border credit flows in major reserve currencies — a complement to domestic money stocks, not a substitute. The International Monetary Fund collects “broad money” across roughly 190 countries, but uses inconsistent country-level definitions and publishes with a significant lag. Bloomberg's terminal offers a commercial global M2 composite (the .glmosupp index) that institutional analysts rely on, but access costs run to tens of thousands of dollars annually. Without Bloomberg, a macro analyst is left hand-aggregating central bank releases and making their own currency-conversion choices — hardly a reproducible methodology.

The stakes of this gap become concrete in gold-price analysis. VanEck published a paper in January 2026 exploring what gold would be worth if it “backed” global reserve liabilities. Using Bloomberg's global M2 figure and IMF counts of official central bank gold holdings — approximately 1.2 billion troy ounces — VanEck derived an implied equilibrium near $100,000 per ounce unweighted, falling to roughly $39,000 using the narrower *M0* monetary base weighted by each currency's share of global foreign-exchange trading. These are valuation anchors, not price targets: they ask how much money exists per unit of gold. The calculation depends on a reliable global M2 input — which is precisely what the tweet says is missing.

Michael Howell of CrossBorderCapital argues that even a complete global M2 would understate real monetary conditions. His firm's *GL Indexes* span more than 90 economies and include wholesale *repo* markets, collateral chains, and shadow-banking capacity — running at roughly two and a half times the size of global M2. Howell's research finds that these broader liquidity flows *Granger-cause* movements in gold and Bitcoin prices, meaning the signal statistically precedes the price move; global M2 alone does not pass the same test. By his account, markets are increasingly driven by credit-creation mechanisms that central banks' deposit-based money-stock figures were never designed to capture.

concepts.definition: A measure of the US money supply that includes physical currency, demand deposits, savings accounts, small certificates of deposit, and retail money-market fund shares. Published weekly by the Federal Reserve via its H.6 release. The Fed stopped treating it as a policy target in the early 1990s but it remains the most-cited domestic liquidity gauge.

An informal aggregate of broad money supply across multiple central banks — typically the Fed, ECB, PBOC, and Bank of Japan at minimum — converted to US dollars at current exchange rates. No official or freely accessible version exists; analysts either hand-build it from central bank releases or rely on Bloomberg's commercial .glmosupp composite index.

The narrowest measure of money: physical currency in circulation plus commercial bank reserves held at the central bank. Also called base money. Central banks can expand or contract M0 directly through asset purchases or reserve requirements, whereas broader aggregates like M2 depend on commercial bank lending behavior.

The US Treasury's primary account at the Federal Reserve, where tax revenues are deposited and from which government payments are made. Large drawdowns inject cash into the banking system and mechanically boost M2 even when monetary policy is unchanged, while rebuilds have the opposite effect — creating M2 swings that reflect fiscal dynamics, not global liquidity.

A Federal Reserve facility that allows money-market funds and other counterparties to park cash at the Fed overnight in exchange for US Treasury securities, earning a set interest rate. Large RRP balances effectively remove money from the banking system, suppressing M2. As those balances drain, M2 rises — again with no direct implication for global conditions.

A quarterly dataset published by the Bank for International Settlements tracking cross-border credit extended in major reserve currencies (dollar, euro, yen) to borrowers outside each currency's home country. They measure international lending flows, not domestic money stocks, and are not a substitute for a consolidated global M2 figure.

Proprietary global liquidity indices published by CrossBorderCapital, covering more than 90 economies. They incorporate repo markets, collateral chains, and shadow-banking flows in addition to central bank balance sheets, and run at roughly two and a half times the size of aggregate global M2.

Short for repurchase agreement market: a market where financial institutions borrow cash short-term by posting securities as collateral and agreeing to repurchase them at a slightly higher price. Repo is a critical source of wholesale short-term funding and a major component of total financial system liquidity that M2 does not capture.

A statistical test developed by economist Clive Granger that asks whether past values of one variable reliably predict future values of another beyond what the second variable predicts on its own. If X Granger-causes Y, changes in X consistently precede changes in Y. It is a stronger claim than correlation but does not establish economic mechanism.

Credit intermediation that occurs outside the traditional regulated banking system — through money-market funds, hedge funds, securities dealers, and structured vehicles. Shadow banks create credit and liquidity but hold no central bank reserves, so their activity is largely invisible in M2 figures.

The European Central Bank, the monetary authority for the 20 eurozone member states. It publishes its own M2 and M3 aggregates for the eurozone, but these must be separately aggregated (and currency-converted) to contribute to any global M2 figure.

The People's Bank of China, China's central bank. It publishes M2 data in yuan, making it the world's largest single-country M2 aggregate by some measures — yet it is excluded from most casual references to “M2” in Western financial media, which default to the US figure.

fact_check: The tweet describes US M2 as “just US reserves,” which conflates two distinct monetary concepts. Bank reserves — funds commercial banks hold at the Federal Reserve — are a component of the narrow M0 monetary base, not of M2. M2 is a much broader aggregate covering household deposits, money-market fund shares, and small certificates of deposit. The intended point — that M2 as commonly cited captures only the American monetary zone — is correct; “reserves” is simply an imprecise word choice for “domestic data.”

sources.note: Official weekly US M2 series back to 1959; baseline for understanding what the commonly cited figure measures and what it omits.

sources.title: Bitcoin: A Global Liquidity Barometer — Lyn Alden
sources.note: Primary source for the 83% correlation claim and the eight-country global M2 methodology; best public practitioner explanation of why global M2 predicts asset prices better than US M2 alone.

sources.title: If The Dollar Loses Reserve Status, Could Gold Surpass $39k? — VanEck (via Seeking Alpha)
sources.note: VanEck paper using Bloomberg global M2 and IMF gold reserve data to derive implied gold price equilibria at M0 (~$39k) and M2 (~$100k) levels; primary source for the gold valuation anchors in the body.

sources.title: Global Liquidity Indicators — BIS Data Portal
sources.note: Confirms that the BIS does not publish a consolidated global M2; its GLIs measure cross-border credit flows, an adjacent but distinct concept.

sources.title: Major Central Bank M2 Comparison — MacroMicro
sources.note: Free public aggregation of the four-bank global M2 (Fed + ECB + PBOC + BOJ) with explanation of the exchange-rate distortion problem.

sources.title: Capital Wars Substack — Michael Howell / CrossBorderCapital
sources.note: Primary source for the GL Indexes methodology, the claim that global liquidity runs 2.5x global M2, and the Granger-causality finding linking broader liquidity measures to gold and Bitcoin.
